transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-28
Time: 2:00 PM PT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Lisa Gomez (Meridian Head of MLOps), Tom Bradford (Meridian CTO), Nina Park (Eng Manager)

Summary:
Quick demo of Redwood structured output (JSON mode) + function calling / tool integration. Focus on schemas, guardrails, and how Console + Optimize help keep quality while controlling cost/latency. Agreed next steps: pricing, security docs, and a pilot/baseline benchmark.

Topics:
- Structured output & JSON schemas
- Function/tool calling and integrations (internal services, ticketing)
- Console demos: schema editor, guardrail rules, tracing
- Redwood Optimize: batching / quantization recommendations and cost tradeoffs
- Deployment options: hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC) and security concerns (SOC2, KMS)

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Ava (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Ava, AE on the account, and with me is Ravi our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Lisa (Meridian): Good, thanks. We're excited to see the JSON mode and function call flow - should be relevant to our merch ops pipelines.
[00:12] Tom (Meridian): Yep, short on time today but want to see end-to-end and understand perf implications.
[00:18] Ravi (Redwood-SE): Great. I'll start with a quick overview, then jump into the Console demo showing schema enforcement, guardrails, and an example function call to our ticketing API. If at any point you have Qs, stop me.
[00:30] Ravi: So structured output in Redwood means you can pin a schema for the model to emit JSON. It runs client-side validations and we have runtime guardrails so if the model strays we either reject or coerce based on policy. Example: product_reco schema with fields product_id, score, reason.
[00:50] Lisa: Quick Q — is the validation happening in the same request path? Any extra latency?
[00:55] Ravi: Good question. Validation is synchronous but lightweight; for typical JSON payloads it's sub-10ms. The heavy part is model inference. If you use our hosted API with streaming it's negligible. If you're on dedicated with quantized models it's similar, but depends on batch sizes.
[01:12] Tom: What about retries/fallbacks if schema fails? We can't have downstream crashes.
[01:16] Ava: We have config options — fail-fast, repair-and-return, or fallback to a simpler model variant. Most enterprises use repair with a sanitized output and also log the incident to the audit trail.
[01:28] Nina: Can you show an example of the guardrail? Like types and enumerations?
[01:32] Ravi: Sure — switching screens. (share) Here in Console you can author a JSON schema, add rules: enums, regex, numeric ranges. You can also add a confidence threshold that triggers a fallback. I'll run a demo prompt now.
[01:50] [01:50] Ravi: Prompting: "Given user context, return purchase recommendations in product_reco schema"... Model emits valid JSON per schema. You can see the trace: tokens, latency, model variant.
[02:05] Lisa: That trace view is great. Can we attach a custom validator? We have business rules that aren't expressible as plain schema.
[02:11] Ravi: Yes — you can plug in a webhook or a lambda. We support function calling where the model calls a defined function name with JSON args; Redwood can execute the function (in hosted) or route it to your private endpoint for on-prem.
[02:25] Tom: So function calling — is Redwood executing our service or just returning the function call payload?
[02:30] Ravi: Both patterns supported. In hosted, we can execute via an integration (e.g., JIRA, ServiceNow) or call your endpoint with mTLS if you set up a private integration. Otherwise the API returns the function call payload and your app executes it.
[02:43] [02:43] Ava: A typical flow is model returns action suggestion -> Redwood optionally executes -> logs action in audit trail -> you can enable approvals.
[02:52] Nina: How do we secure the function endpoints? We can't expose internal services.
[02:56] Ravi: For Private deployments or VPC peering we do mutual TLS and you can put an internal NAT. We also support customer-managed keys for payload encryption (KMS/HSM).
[03:10] Lisa: SOC2 and logs — we need full auditability.
[03:13] Ava: We provide audit logs, per-request tracing, and you can push logs to your SIEM. We have an enterprise compliance pack including SOC2 docs and options for on-prem control plane. I'll share the whitepaper.
[03:24] [03:24] Tom: Ok show me the API call pattern for JSON mode.
[03:27] Ravi: Example: POST /v1/generate with body containing schema and tool definitions. You can set mode=json and function_definitions. The response either returns structured JSON or a function_call object. (shows code snippet)
[03:40] Ravi: Here's the SDK pattern — you specify schema, tolerance level, and a fallback policy. You can also turn on strict_mode which rejects anything not conforming.
[03:50] Lisa: If strict_mode rejects too often, we'll lose throughput. Can Optimize help tune that?
[03:55] Ravi: Redwood Optimize looks at your traffic and suggests batching, quantization, and model variants to hit latency/cost targets while preserving quality. For example, for chatty low-latency endpoints we recommend small batch sizes with a 16-bit quantized variant; for bulk re-ranking we suggest larger batches and different kernels.
[04:15] [04:15] Tom: What are the unit costs for hosted vs dedicated? We have predictable traffic spikes in holiday season.
[04:20] Ava: Hosted is usage-based per token; Dedicated is reserved capacity with a monthly commitment and burst options. We'll include a pricing sheet but a rough rule of thumb: dedicated becomes cost-effective at sustained throughput above X tokens per second — we'll quantify in the follow-up.
[04:36] Nina: Any vendor lock-in with annotated schemas or tooling?
[04:39] Ravi: Schemas are standard JSON Schema; policies and traces are exportable. You can export snapshots and run on your own runtime if you opt for Private. The model artifacts are upstream (open models or customer-supplied).
[04:50] [04:50] Ava: Moving on to a function-calling example integrated to a ticketing system. Ravi, remind them what we built for a retail customer previously.
[04:58] Ravi: Sure — we had model suggest actions and call create_ticket function. Example: function create_ticket({product_id, issue_type, severity}) which maps to their internal ticketing. In the demo I'll call a mocked endpoint.
[05:10] [05:10] Ravi: Triggering the prompt... model decides to call create_ticket, returns function_call payload. In our hosted demo I'm going to auto-execute the call so you can see the end-to-end flow.
[05:25] Lisa: Nice. Where does the data residency element sit? We are EU and NA customers.
[05:29] Ava: For hosted we have regional endpoints and can pin data region. For strict residency you can choose Private deployment.
[05:35] Tom: How about latency numbers — do you have p50/p95 on A100 vs T4?
[05:40] Ravi: We maintain published benchmarks. Roughly p50 on A100 is 120ms for the model we demoed with seq length 256; p95 around 300ms. On T4 it can be 2-3x depending on quant. That said Optimize can recommend kernel/quant trades to hit your SLOs.
[05:58] [05:58] Lisa: For our use case we have 90% of requests under 200ms requirement.
[06:02] Ravi: We can engineer for that with dedicated capacity and smaller batch sizes, and fallback to a cheaper but faster model for non-critical paths.
[06:10] Nina: Can we get token-level cost breakdowns per route?
[06:13] Ava: Yes — Console shows per-route token breakdown and you can set per-route budgets.
[06:20] [06:20] Tom: Any caveats around KV cache during function calling? We have lots of repeated context keys.
[06:25] Ravi: KV cache is per-session; for function calling we preserve kv across calls unless you explicitly s flush. Cache hits are a big win for repeated contexts.
[06:34] [06:34] Lisa: Show the guardrail triggering and an example where model violates schema and we repair.
[06:38] Ravi: Running a purposely malformed prompt... model returns string for numeric field. Repair policy kicks in: we coerce to null and add a warning in the trace. You can route those warnings to an alerts endpoint.
[06:52] Ava: Customers often use that to feed failing cases into a retrain or fine-tune queue.
[06:58] [06:58] Nina: Let's talk pilot scope — what will the benchmark look like?
[07:02] Ava: We propose: 1) baseline run on your sample prompts across two models, 2) throughput run on dedicated config, 3) quality eval against your metrics. We'll do a joint run and present results.
[07:16] Lisa: For quality, we care about precision@3 for product recs and low hallucination rate.
[07:21] Ravi: We'll wire up a simple eval harness and run it.
[07:25] [07:25] Tom: Cost control — is there automatic throttling if we exceed committed capacity?
[07:29] Ava: Yes. We support burst buckets and policy-based throttling with graceful degradation—fallback to cheaper model or queueing depending on config.
[07:37] Nina: Can you show the Optimize UI suggestions?
[07:40] Ravi: (shares Optimize screen) Here it analyzes recent traffic and suggests quantization to 8-bit for non-critical routes, recommends batch sizes, and estimates token savings. You can accept suggestions and we provide a simulation of expected latency/cost.
[07:58] [07:58] Lisa: A couple of security questions — do you support SAML SSO and role-based access? We need per-team RBAC.
[08:03] Ava: Yes SAML/SCIM, RBAC with custom roles, and audit logs tied to tokens. For more sensitive data, you can enable customer-managed KMS.
[08:12] Tom: What about model versioning and rollouts?
[08:15] Ravi: Console supports canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automatic rollback on regression signals. You can pin routes to model versions.
[08:23] [08:23] Nina: If we want an on-prem control plane what changes?
[08:26] Ava: The private option moves the control plane into your VPC or on-prem env; data plane can remain in our infra if you prefer. There are additional compliance and support SLAs. We'll detail that in the doc pack.
[08:38] [08:38] Tom: Ok let's look at an example where model needs to call multiple tools in a single response — e.g., price lookup then create ticket.
[08:44] Ravi: We support sequential tool calls. The model can emit function_call A, we execute/return result, then model continues and emits function_call B. There are timeout controls and max-call limits.
[08:57] Lisa: Any limits on function call payload size? We have large product metadata.
[09:02] Ravi: We advise passing IDs and retrieving heavy payloads server-side. But we do support larger payloads up to configured limits; for very large blobs we recommend prefetching or using object storage links.
[09:14] [09:14] Ava: Switching back to the Console — I'll demo the Schema Editor where you can import existing JSON Schemas and add human readable rules.
[09:22] Ravi: Also note the trace shows token-level attribution so you can see why the model picked a field value. Helpful for debugging hallucinations.
[09:31] Nina: For the pilot, can we get a list of the required infra on our side?
[09:35] Ava: Minimal for hosted: nothing, we just need sample data and endpoints for function calls if you want execution. For dedicated/private we'll share a checklist: VPC peering, NAT, firewall rules, and KMS connectivity. We'll include that in follow-up.
[09:50] [09:50] Tom: Got it. Any data retention options? We need logs for 1 year.
[09:55] Ava: Retention is configurable per contract; we can set log retention to a year and push to your S3 or SIEM.
[10:03] [10:03] Lisa: Are there customer references in retail who used this exact flow?
[10:06] Ravi: Yes — we built a similar flow for Meridian Retail — improved auto-ticketing and reduced manual triage by 40%. We can connect you.
[10:15] [10:15] Tom: Let's recap next steps.
[10:17] Ava: Recap: we'll send pricing and Dedicated options, SOC2 pack, and proposed pilot plan. Ravi will run a benchmark and Lisa will send sample prompts.
[10:25] Lisa: Sounds good.
[10:27] Nina: One more Q — can we schedule a SE deep-dive for infra/network on Aug 4?
[10:32] Ava: I'll set it up.
[10:34] [10:34] Ava: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email and Slack.

Closing notes: action items captured above. Meeting ended at ~2:46 PM PT.
